processing: Typical of Fenghuang Dancong: sun-withered, shaken and rested to partial oxidation, fired, rolled and dried or lightly roasted.
harvest_season: As with most Fenghuang Dancong, spring is the main picking; sellers list it by harvest year.
appearance_dry: Typically long, tight, dark brown strips, as with other Dancong.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear golden to orange, as with other honey-orchid Dancong.
appearance_wet: Typically long leaves, green with reddened edges, as with other Dancong.
taste_profile: Named for a smell like fragrant sweet potato when brewed. Its honey-orchid group is generally known for a honeyed sweetness.

brewing.notes: As with other Dancong, keep steeps very short. Smell the empty cup, where the sweet potato note may be easiest to find.

vintage_note: Specialist sellers list it by harvest year as a Chaozhou Dancong, for example as a 2026 lot. As is usual for the class, it is sold from the most recent spring, sometimes after extra months of rest.
description:
Sweet potato is an unusual thing to name a tea after, but that is the story here. A Chinese article on Dancong aroma groups says Song Zhong Mi Lan Xiang was originally called Fanshu Xiang because the brewed tea smelled just like fragrant sweet potato.

That places it in the honey-orchid (mi lan) group, one of the best known in Fenghuang. Processing would follow the usual Dancong path of sun withering, shaking, firing and rolling.

Much of the character here has to be taken from the name and the group: a warm, sweet aroma with honey in the cup. Brew it in a gaiwan with quick pours, since Dancong punish long steeps with bitterness.

'Song Zhong' on the label implies old-tree material, so ask what the claim rests on.
history: Fan Shu Xiang is described as the original name of Song Zhong Mi Lan Xiang. When the name changed and who selected the tree are not recorded in anything readily available.
